name: Mangalapureeswarar Temple, Thiruchopuram
deity: Shiva as Mangalapureeswarar (Chopuranathar), with the goddess Thyagavalli (Velnedunkanni)
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Nadu Nadu near the Coromandel coast south of Cuddalore, sung by Sambandar in the Tevaram (7th century)
dynasty: Chola, with renovation traditionally credited to Queen Thyagavalli of Kulothunga I
summary: Near the coast south of Cuddalore, in a temple once buried by drifting dunes, Shiva is worshipped as Mangalapureeswarar in a lingam of sea sand said to bear the palm prints of the sage Agastya.

sections.history: Thiruchopuram lies in the coastal country about 20 km south of Cuddalore, in the village now called Thiyagavalli. Its Shiva temple is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and is counted among the shrines of Nadu Nadu; Thirugnana Sambandar sang it in a pathigam preserved in the First Thirumurai. The village name is linked with Thyagavalli, chief queen of the Chola emperor Kulothunga I, who is believed to have renovated the temple. Tradition also remembers a time when the shrine lay buried under the sand of the shore, until a devotee glimpsed the finial of its tower and the villagers dug it free.
sections.architecture: The heart of the temple is its lingam, said to be fashioned of sea sand. It rests on a square pedestal, with a small rounded form at the top that devotees take to be the Ganga, and its surface is said to carry the impressions of Agastya's palms. Around it stand the enclosures of a Dravidian village temple, with a separate shrine for the goddess Thyagavalli, also called Velnedunkanni, she of the long, spear-like eyes.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells that Agastya, wishing to worship Shiva on this shore, shaped a lingam from sea sand, but it would not keep its form. Understanding this as the Lord's play, he mixed the juice of herbs with the sand, and the lingam held. Tradition adds that Parvati merged into the lingam here, making it auspicious, mangala — hence Mangalapureeswarar — and so devotees receive kumkumam and turmeric as prasadam rather than sacred ash.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri in Masi, Thirukarthigai in the month of Karthigai, the Aippasi Annabhishekam and Panguni Uthiram are the temple's main observances, with the monthly Pradosham. Because the goddess is held to dwell within the lingam itself, the days of Navaratri carry a special warmth here. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Come to Thiruchopuram for the rare sight of a sand lingam and the quiet of a coastal village. Look closely at the form of the lingam, receive the kumkumam that marks the goddess's presence within it, and remember the dunes that once hid the whole temple. It pairs easily with the nearby shrine at Theerthanagiri and with the temples of Cuddalore.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most village temples of the region. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer areas, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruchopuram (Thiyagavalli) is about 20 km south of Cuddalore, reached by local buses and hired cars from Cuddalore. Cuddalore has the nearest convenient railway stations; Puducherry is the nearest airport, with Chennai the nearest major international airport.
